idiom_name: kotlin.test / JUnit 5 + committed golden resources, hand-written compare/update (Paparazzi or Roborazzi for UI goldens)
implementation_notes: kotlin.test provides annotations and assertions bound to a JVM framework through kotlin-test-junit5, but neither it nor JUnit stores snapshots, so the JVM story is the Java one and the loop is hand-written: capture the subject's output, read the committed golden from the source tree or test resources, compare with assertEquals and gate rewriting behind a system property or a dedicated recorder test. For Android UI the dominant realization is different and library-shaped - render the screen headlessly and compare the image against a recorded baseline with Paparazzi or Roborazzi, whose Gradle tasks (record/verify) supply the approval step. The hand-written form remains the right default for pure JVM logic and small text artefacts, and data classes make it pleasant as long as you pin an explicit rendering rather than the generated toString.
pitfalls: Android screenshot goldens must be recorded through the library's Gradle task, not from an instrumented test on a device: the app sandbox is not the repository, so writes from the test process are lost or land in the wrong place.
Kotlin data-class toString prints every property with its name and includes nested collections; pin an explicit, stable rendering or a data class refactor breaks the golden.
JVM default locale and timezone leak into formatting and are machine-dependent; fix Locale.ROOT and a timezone in the test setup.
